headline: SNDL renews share buyback at up to C$100M after retiring 24.5M shares
dek: SNDL retired 24.5 million shares in the year to 20 November, its full limit, and approved a new buyback of up to C$100 million or 23.6 million shares.
key_points: SNDL repurchased 24,488,322 shares between 21 November 2025 and 20 November 2026, using 100% of the shares its previous program allowed.
The new program, effective 23 November 2026 to 22 November 2027, allows up to C$100 million of purchases, capped at about 23,573,925 shares, or 10% of the public float.
At recent share prices the share cap, not the dollar cap, is the real limit: 23.6 million shares would cost far less than C$100 million.
The renewal sits beside a proposed tender offer of up to C$50 million and a cash pile of C$617.8 million with no debt, reported in October.
body: SNDL, the Canadian cannabis and liquor retailer, has renewed its share buyback after using every share its last program allowed. In an announcement on 23 November, the Nasdaq-listed company said it repurchased 24,488,322 common shares under the program that ran from 21 November 2025 to 20 November 2026, according to The Marijuana Herald's report of the release. That was 10% of the public float when the program began and 100% of what it was permitted to buy.

The new authorization allows SNDL to buy up to C$100 million of its own shares at market prices from 23 November 2026 to 22 November 2027. It is also capped by share count: no more than about 23,573,925 shares, again 10% of the public float at the start. Shares bought will be cancelled, and the company is not obliged to buy any minimum amount.

A buyback with both a dollar limit and a share limit stops at whichever is reached first. On our arithmetic, C$100 million spread across 23.57 million shares works out to about C$4.24 a share. SNDL's stock has been trading far below that: Business of Cannabis's delayed tracker showed it at US$1.26 on 23 November. At prices near that level, buying the full 23.6 million shares would cost only a fraction of C$100 million, so the share cap is the binding limit unless the price rises several times over.

The two float figures also show how far the share count has moved. The old program's 24.49 million shares were 10% of the float in November 2025, implying a float of roughly 244.9 million shares then. The new limit of 23.57 million implies about 235.7 million now, a fall of roughly 9.1 million shares, or about 3.7%. The drop is smaller than the 24.5 million shares bought back, which suggests other changes to the float over the year, such as share issuance or reclassification; the release as reported does not explain the difference.
Purchases can be made on the open market, through privately negotiated deals, block trades and other permitted methods. SNDL can suspend or end the program at management's discretion.
> SNDL is treating its own shares as its best-priced acquisition. The test is whether the cash would earn more anywhere else in a cheap cannabis market.

SNDL can afford to do this because it carries no debt. As we reported on 6 November, the company ended the third quarter with C$617.8 million in unrestricted cash and investments, posted record free cash flow of C$20.0 million (C$10.6 million of it from a one-time insurance unwind) and proposed a separate share tender of up to C$50 million. The renewed buyback adds a second, slower channel for returning capital to holders.

The same quarter showed why investors have been cautious. Revenue fell 2.5% to C$238.0 million, and a C$52 million noncash impairment in cannabis operations pushed the company to a C$48.3 million operating loss. Retail did the heavy lifting: cannabis retail, run under the Value Buds and Spiritleaf banners, and liquor retail both reported record gross margins of 27.0%. Management is reviewing the cultivation business, with options from asset sales to productivity programs.

On 10 November we reported that SNDL's Atholville, New Brunswick site won EU-GMP certification for producing and packaging medical flower for export. That gives the review a more saleable asset, or a route into Europe, whichever way it goes.

Few cannabis companies are in a position to buy back stock. As we reported on 15 November, five large US multi-state operators carry a combined $1.96 billion in disputed Section 280E tax liabilities. SNDL, by contrast, has a large net cash position and an investment portfolio spanning the North American cannabis industry, the Herald noted, alongside its retail businesses.

Shrinking the share count lifts each remaining share's claim on that cash and on future earnings. The open question is the price. If the market is valuing SNDL well below its cash and investments, as its supporters argue, buybacks are a cheap way to capture that gap. If the cannabis operations keep losing money, cash spent on shares cannot be spent on fixing them.
SNDL shares rose 7.7% on 23 November on Business of Cannabis's delayed tracker. We do not read much into one day's move; the program's effect will show in the share count each quarter.

The next quarterly report will show how many shares SNDL bought under the new program and at what average price, and whether the proposed C$50 million tender goes ahead. Watch also for the outcome of the review of the cultivation business, which will decide how much of SNDL's future cash goes to its own shares rather than to its plants.
